I am 65 years old and have been farming these 8 mu in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My father taught me everything I know, and I have never gone to school, but the land and the seasons are my teachers. I do not try newfangled things I see on the internet — I do what my neighbors do and what the seed shop in town tells me, because that is how we survive here on the North China Plain.

This year, just like every year, I will grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation. That is the only system that makes sense on this flat land with our groundwater well. I cannot afford to leave the field idle, and the wheat comes off in early June, which gives me just enough time to plant maize right behind the harvester. My son helps me hire a combine for the wheat, and then we seed the maize directly into the stubble without ploughing — my back is not what it used to be, and no-tillage saves me labor and diesel. For the wheat, I will still run the rotary tiller once before sowing in early October, because the soil gets hard over the summer and the wheat roots need a loose bed.

For seeds, I buy improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed from the dealer every year. I do not save my own seed — the yield drops too much, and the hybrids do not breed true. The shopkeeper recommended a new wheat variety last autumn, but I stuck to the one I know; for maize I usually take whatever hybrid they have in stock, like Nongda 372 or Denghai 605, because they stand up to the wind and give me around 1,100 jin per mu.

Fertilizer is expensive, but if you skimp, the yield punishes you. I put down a bag of compound fertilizer as basal for both crops — about 50 kg per mu for wheat and 40 kg per mu for maize — and then I topdress urea when the wheat starts jointing and again for the maize when it is knee-high. I do not measure everything exactly; I go by the bag size and what my neighbors spread. I also irrigate from my well using border flooding: three times for wheat — once before winter, once at jointing, and once at grain filling — and twice for maize, once right after sowing and once at the big trumpet-leaf stage. 

For chemicals, I spray herbicide once for each crop, fungicide once on the wheat, and insecticide two or three times when the bugs show up. That is what I have always done, and it keeps the fields clean enough.
